Any existing code in the repository that constructs InsightsBookingService and calls `findMany(...)` to fetch bookings will now fail at compile time (or worse, at runtime if untyped) with 'findMany is not a function'. The PR description only mentions test updates, so this removal appears to be an unannounced breaking API change. Either keep `findMany` (implemented via $queryRaw with the base conditions) or update all call sites in the same PR.

Tests were never executed; PR author reports test runner failures

The PR's own review checklist states 'I encountered test runner configuration issues, so please verify the tests actually pass.' None of the assertions in this file — especially the structural `toEqual(Prisma.sql\`...\`)` comparisons and the `$queryRaw` query against "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" — have been confirmed to pass. Notably, `$queryRaw` in Postgres returns BigInt for bigint columns, so the `expect(results).toEqual([{ id: userBooking.id }])` comparison at line 487 will fail if the table's id column is bigint, and the denormalized table must be populated (e.g. by trigger) for the booking created via `prisma.booking.create` for the row to appear at all. These tests must be run and confirmed green before merging.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

The comment says it updates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt, but an empty `data` object contains no fields, so Prisma will either fail validation ("at least one field") or perform a no-op; in either case `updatedAt` is not bumped because @updatedAt is only refreshed when an update actually writes fields. true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

deleteCacheHandler throws plain Error instead of a TRPCError, producing an opaque internal server error

Throw a TRPCError with code UNAUTHORIZED/NOT_FOUND instead. Also note that for delegated (in-memory) credentials the UI passes a negative credentialId which will always land on this error path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Behavior change: Alert rows now hide disconnect button when disableConnectionModification is set

Previously, the error/Alert branch rendered the disconnect control whenever `!connectedCalendar.delegationCredentialId` regardless of `disableConnectionModification`; the new CredentialActionsDropdown applies `disableConnectionModification` in both branches, so users in contexts that pass that flag (e.g. certain embed/event-type scopes) lose the ability to remove a broken integration from the Alert row where it was previously available. The handler unconditionally instantiates CalendarCacheRepository and runs a groupBy over calendarCache for all credentialIds on every invocation of this very hot query (used by onboarding, settings, booking pages). Consider guarding the extra round-trip (e.g. only query when there is at least one Google Calendar credential, or fold the max(updatedAt) into the existing credential fetch) to avoid adding latency to every connectedCalendars request.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status

After a successful cache deletion the component only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback (which in SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper is `props.onChanged` and may be undefined). Unlike the disconnect mutation, there is no `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()`, so the "Cache Status / Last updated" entry in the dropdown keeps showing the old timestamp until a full page reload or unrelated refetch. Add the same invalidation used in disconnectMutation's onSettled.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation calls are fire-and-forget; request can complete before DB updates persist

The old code collected the reminder deletions into `prismaPromises` and awaited them via `Promise.all` before responding. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside a `forEach` without awaiting any of them. These functions perform DB writes (`cancelled: true` update or row delete) and external API calls; on a serverless deployment the function can be frozen/terminated right after the response is returned, so the `cancelled` flag may never be persisted — the scheduled email would still be sent for the cancelled booking. The same unawaited-forEach pattern was introduced in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule, ~line 488) and `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts` (~line 966), where the surrounding try/catch also cannot catch the async rejections. Await these calls (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves the WorkflowReminder row in scheduled state

When `immediateDelete` is true and a referenceId exists, the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting or flagging the DB row. Callers like the workflow `delete` mutation rely on DB cascade to remove rows, but callers that don't cascade (e.g. edited workflow steps in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx`) leave a row with `scheduled: true`, `cancelled: null` and a live referenceId until the CRON's past-date cleanup deletes it. Any future query that assumes `scheduled: true` means 'an active send exists' (or that re-reads and re-cancels) will operate on stale state. Deleting the row in this branch (as done for SMS) would make the semantics consistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation query includes unscheduled reminders, and one SendGrid failure aborts all remaining cancellations

The query selecting `remindersToCancel` filters only on `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now+1h`, without filtering `scheduled: true` (or method EMAIL). Reminders that were marked cancelled while still unscheduled (`scheduled: false`) have `referenceId: null`, so the SendGrid request `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: null` will fail. Because the entire for-loop is wrapped in a single try/catch, that first failure throws out of the loop and none of the remaining cancelled reminders are cancelled at SendGrid — their scheduled emails will still be sent, which is exactly the bug this PR claims to fix. Filter to scheduled reminders with a non-null referenceId, and handle failures per-reminder instead of aborting the batch.

Deferred cancellation window leaves reminders due within ~15 minutes still sent

In the non-immediate path, cancelling a scheduled email only sets `cancelled: true`; the actual SendGrid cancellation happens in the CRON job, which (per the PR description) runs every 15 minutes and only cancels reminders whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. A booking cancelled when its reminder is due in less than one cron interval (e.g. 5 minutes from now) will not be cancelled before the scheduled send time — the email/SMS reminder is still delivered for a cancelled or rescheduled booking. The previous behaviour cancelled immediately at SendGrid. Either cancel immediately when scheduledDate is within the cron interval, or run cancellation more frequently / without the 1-hour window.

Prisma delete promises created in loop but only awaited at end; leaked on error

Inside the cancellation loop, `prisma.workflowReminder.delete({...})` is called (creating the query promise) and pushed to an array, but the array is only awaited after the loop. If any SendGrid cancel request throws (see the surrounding try/catch that aborts the loop), the already-created delete promises are never awaited, so those rows are never deleted (and Prisma query promises left unawaited keep the connection busy / are silently dropped). The reminder rows would then be retried on the next cron run. Delete each row right after its successful cancellation, or wrap each iteration in its own try/catch.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-booking calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes asynchronously and never awaited

In the `allRemainingBookings` path, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... const deletedEvent = await calendar?.deleteEvent(...); apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` uses an async callback inside forEach. The push into `apiDeletes` happens only after the await, i.e. on a later microtask/macrotask tick, while the surrounding handler continues and reaches `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) before the forEach callbacks have pushed anything. Previously (with the sync `getCalendar`) the deleteEvent promise was pushed synchronously and thus awaited. As a result, cancellation of all remaining recurring events returns success while the external calendar-event deletions are still in flight (or may never complete if the request/process ends), leaving orphaned events on users' calendars.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so the appStore is not actually lazy and failures become unhandled rejections

`const appStore = { applecalendar: import("./applecalendar"), ... }` calls `import()` at module-evaluation time for every app. This defeats the stated purpose of the PR (async/lazy imports): merely importing `@calcom/app-store` still triggers loading of all ~28 app packages. Worse, if any single app module throws at load time, its promise rejects with no `.catch` anywhere, producing an unhandled promise rejection at startup (a hard crash under Node's default behavior). To be lazy, the store should expose getters or functions (e.g. `get applecalendar() { return import("./applecalendar") }`) so imports only run on access.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check compares slot end minutes to slot start minutes

In the newly added working-hours check inside checkIfIsAvailable, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start` two lines above. Because of this, the condition `end > workingHour.endTime` can never be true, so slots that start inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) exceeds the end of the working hours are incorrectly reported as available. The `end` computation should include the event length, e.g. `start + eventLength`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === never match, breaking 'unavailable' date overrides

In checkIfIsAvailable the guard for a full-day block is `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")`. Dayjs factory calls always return distinct object instances, so this strict equality is never true regardless of the underlying times. The intended 'start equals end means mark the whole day unavailable' case is therefore never detected: for a blocked day, a slot that spans the block timestamp falls through all the other conditions, find() returns undefined, dateOverrideExist is true, and the function returns true (available). Result: slots overlapping an 'unavailable' date override are still shown as bookable. Use .isSame() (or compare .valueOf()) instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override day match compares organizer-local date against UTC slot date

In checkIfIsAvailable, the override's day is computed by converting `date.start` into the organizer's wall-clock time (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')`) but it is compared against `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`, which is the slot's UTC date. When the organizer's timezone is not UTC, the two dates only coincide by accident; for organizers east of UTC an override late in their local day maps to the next UTC day's slots and vice versa, so overrides apply to (or are skipped for) the wrong day. The slot date should be converted to the organizer timezone (e.g. dayjs.tz(slotStartTime, organizerTimeZone)) before the comparison.

No test for the primary fix: round-robin date overrides of fixed hosts

The PR's headline fix (#8207) is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected for round-robin events, implemented via the new dateOverrides/workingHours logic in checkIfIsAvailable and the isFixed filtering in getSchedule. The only test added is the timezone-variation case for a personal event's date override. There is no test with a ROUND_ROBIN event containing a fixed host with a date override (the scenario described in the PR's own manual test plan), so a regression in the fixed-host filtering (e.g. the working-hours minutes bug above) would go undetected. Add a test mirroring the manual steps: round-robin event, one fixed host with an override, one round-robin host, assert only fixed-host-available slots are returned.

Override minute conversion drops day information and can produce inverted ranges

The new offset conversion computes startTime/endTime as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + .minute()`. Only the wall-clock hour/minute of the shifted instant is kept, so when the timezone offset shifts the override into the previous or next calendar day relative to the invitee day being computed, the resulting minute value silently wraps around midnight: an override whose shifted start is 23:30 yields startTime=1410 while endTime (shifted to 00:30 next day) yields 30, giving startTime > endTime. buildSlots then discards the range ('bypass invalid value' when start >= end), so the override disappears and the day falls back to nothing (the user's normal working hours for that day were already spliced out), leaving zero availability instead of the override window. The calculation should also adjust for the day shift (e.g. compare dates and add/subtract 24h of minutes).

Override offset computed via Date.toString() parsed in server-local timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` stringifies the Date in the server's local timezone and re-parses it with dayjs (also local), then converts to the organizer timezone. Because both the stringify and the parse use the same local zone the instant is approximately preserved, but this is fragile (toString includes a timezone name/offset that dayjs parsing may or may not honor consistently) and it is simpler and safer to use `dayjs(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()`. Additionally, `override.timeZone` is optional in the TimeRange type; if a caller omits it (e.g. dynamic-event paths or other consumers of getSlots), `dayjs(...).tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the server's local timezone, producing wrong offsets with no error. Consider making it required or defaulting explicitly.

Working-hours minutes compared in different timezones (organizer vs UTC)

The new working-hours check computes `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` from the slot's UTC time and compares it to `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime`. Per the WorkingHours type comment (packages/types/schedule.d.ts), those values are 'minutes since midnight; serialized to UTC by using the organizer timeZone'. So the comparison mixes organizer-local minutes with UTC minutes and is wrong whenever the organizer's timezone is not UTC: for example an organizer in IST with hours 09:30-18:00 local gets workingHour.startTime=570, but a 04:00 UTC slot (09:30 IST) yields 240 < 570 and is rejected, while a 12:00 UTC slot (17:30 IST) passes even though only 30 minutes of the day remain. The slot time must first be converted to the organizer timezone (organizerTimeZone is already passed in) before extracting hour/minute. Note this same mismatch affects the day-of-week check via slotStartTime.day().

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when existing Integration metadata lacks 'sender'

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the user-mismatch check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with no guards. `metadata["sender"]` is only populated when the installation webhook fired before build_integration ran (see build_integration, which only adds `sender` if `state.get("sender")` is set). An existing Integration created without a preceding webhook (e.g. created through the pipeline directly, or older rows predating this flow) has no `sender` key, so this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. Same for a `sender` dict without a `login` key. Use `.get()` with explicit handling (e.g. fail closed with the error page) instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Authorize URL query parameters are not URL-encoded

The redirect URL is built by string interpolation: `f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. The `redirect_uri` value (containing '://' and '/'), `client_id`, and `state` are not URL-encoded. This currently works because the values happen to contain no '&' or '=' characters, but any change to the redirect path or a client_id containing reserved characters would silently corrupt the OAuth request. Use `urlencode` to construct the query string.

Reverse URL built with None installation_id

When GitHub redirects to the setup endpoint with setup_action=install but without an installation_id query parameter (malformed or crafted request), `request.GET.get("installation_id")` returns None and `reverse("integration-installation", args=[provider_id, None])` renders a URL ending in '/github/None'. The user is then redirected to an org-picker URL containing the literal string 'None', which will fail downstream when the pipeline tries to use it. The None case should be handled explicitly (redirect to the app install page or an error) rather than passed into reverse.

State signature compared with non-constant-time equality

The CSRF/anti-replay `state` parameter is validated with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`, a plain string comparison. Since this check is the core of the request-authenticity guarantee introduced by this PR, use `hmac.compare_digest` (or `secrets.compare_digest`) so the comparison is constant-time, matching how other OAuth state validations are typically hardened. Practical exploitability is low, but it is a trivial hardening for a security-focused change.

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(...)` and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` are not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an API call that can raise ApiError (rate limit, 401 for revoked tokens, network errors), and safe_urlopen can raise on connection failures. Any of these will propagate and produce a 500 error page mid-installation instead of the intended 'Invalid installation request.' response, degrading the UX the PR is meant to fix and generating noise in Sentry. The existing try/except only covers the response body parsing, not the requests themselves.

Killed flusher processes are never joined, leaking zombies on repeated restarts

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a hung/crashed process is `kill()`ed and immediately replaced via `_create_process_for_shards`, but `join()` is never called on the old process object (it is simply dropped from `self.processes`). With the spawn start method, killed child processes remain zombies until reaped by the parent. Call `process.join(timeout)` after kill, or otherwise reap the old process before replacing it.

Memory backpressure aggregation across per-process buffers may double-count Redis clusters

`submit()` now aggregates `get_memory_info()` from each per-shard-group buffer. If `get_memory_info()` reports at the Redis cluster/connection level (rather than strictly per shard), clusters whose shards are split across multiple process groups will be counted multiple times in both `used` and `available`, weighting those clusters by how many buffers touch them and skewing the `used/available` ratio used to trigger hard backpressure (pausing the whole consumer). Verify that per-buffer aggregation yields the same totals as the previous single-buffer call for the same shard set; if not, deduplicate by cluster before summing.

An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` (a plausible typo or misconfiguration) will unexpectedly spawn one process per shard rather than getting an error. false_positives.candidate:
A Sentry transaction is started per message in every worker

OrderedQueueWorker wraps every single result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(). At uptime-results throughput this creates an enormous number of transactions (one per Kafka message per worker), which both adds per-message overhead in the hot path and can flood Sentry. The existing code path (ResultProcessor.__call__) already starts a transaction per result, so this doubles transactions per message. Consider a span or sampling.

Offset gaps permanently block commits for a partition

get_committable_offsets stops at the first offset not present in all_offsets and never commits past it. Any offset that is never add_offset'ed for a partition (e.g. messages filtered/dropped upstream of this strategy, or offsets below the initial start after a rebalance where another instance committed some and the tracker's last_committed is stale or -1) creates a permanent gap: all later offsets in that partition become uncommittable, all_offsets grows without bound for the life of the process, and the consumer group's committed lag grows indefinitely, triggering rebalances/max-poll-interval expiry on restart. There is no mechanism to advance past a gap or reset state on partition reassignment.

OffsetTracker state is not reset on partition reassignment/rebalance

The OffsetTracker lives on the shared FixedQueuePool and retains last_committed, all_offsets, and outstanding across rebalances. After a rebalance, create_with_partitions may be invoked with a different partition assignment and the consumer may resume from offsets previously committed by another instance (which can be lower or unrelated to last_committed). If a new message's offset is <= last_committed for that partition, get_committable_offsets returns nothing for it (start = last_committed+1 skips it) and the offset is never committed, stalling that partition's commits. State should be scoped to a strategy/partition assignment lifecycle.

Processing failures are swallowed and offsets still committed (silent data loss)

OrderedQueueWorker.run catches all exceptions from result_processor, logs them, and unconditionally marks the offset complete in the finally block. The commit loop then commits that offset. A permanently failing result (e.g. a bug triggered by a particular payload) is therefore dropped with no retry, no DLQ, and no metric — only a log line. At minimum this should increment a failure metric so operators can detect silent loss; ideally it should integrate with the existing DLQ policy or a retry path.

Rebalance permanently kills the shared queue pool, silently dropping messages

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. But SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() (queue_consumer.py lines 335-345) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and calls queue.shutdown() on every queue. Arroyo calls join()/close() on the old strategy on every rebalance, then calls create_with_partitions again — the new strategy gets the same, now-dead pool. Subsequent submits will raise queue.ShutDown when putting items; that exception is caught by the generic except in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, which marks the offset as complete, so the message is silently dropped and its offset committed. The pool must either be created per-strategy, or the strategy must not shut down the shared pool.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never blocks or signals arroyo to pause (poll() only emits a gauge). The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing fills up. If processing falls behind (the exact scenario this PR is meant to handle — a slow item backlogging a queue), arroyo will keep polling and submitting, and in-memory WorkItems accumulate without bound, risking OOM in the consumer process. Either bound the queues and block/reject submit, or expose a pause/resume mechanism to arroyo.

hash(str) is randomized across processes

get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on a string, which is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). This is fine for ordering within a single process, but any future design where multiple processes (or a restart mid-flight with different assignment) rely on consistent group→queue mapping would silently break ordering assumptions. Using a stable hash (e.g. zlib.crc32 or hashlib) would make the mapping deterministic and document the intent. Low priority since current usage is per-process.

submit() swallows decoder/assert errors and commits offsets for undecodable messages

In submit(), any exception (including the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` failure and decode_payload exceptions) is caught and the offset is immediately marked complete, so the offset is committed even though the message was never processed and no DLQ is involved. This differs from other modes where a decode failure is at least logged with the payload. Combined with the generic ResultProcessor exception swallowing, there are three separate layers of silent-drop with no metric distinguishing 'dropped at decode' from 'dropped at process'.
